## Section 1: Market Overview

*Assumptions: the profile does not say what Acme Advisory sells or who competes with it. The offer comes from the website research. Competitors are inferred from the category and shown as generic types. No external sources were available, so market claims rest on the research documents only. Items to confirm are flagged.*

### 1. Overview (The "Why Now?")

Small and mid-sized companies are already using AI, mostly without a plan. Staff paste client and company data into public chatbots. Leaders know they should act but face two poor options. The first is large consultancies and strategy houses, which are built and priced for enterprises. The second is generic chatbots that forget the business after every session and tie the company to one vendor. Acme Advisory replaces slow, expensive advisory and unmanaged AI use with hands-on guidance from a former product executive, plus tools the client owns.

The mission is to help leaders act faster. A leader can set an AI use policy by answering seven questions. A small team can have an AI operating system running after a one-hour setup (the site's method claim, not yet proven by customer results). A regulated firm can run AI models inside its own office, so client data never leaves. Ease of use and ownership are the design principles. Company knowledge sits in plain files the client controls, and the AI model can be swapped without losing anything. Three tools are free and open source. API access and formal integrations: Not available in the documents.

**Market size (estimates, definitions vary by source):**
- AI consulting: roughly $5B to $11B in 2025.
- Forecast growth: about 17% to 26% a year.
- Acme Advisory's serviceable market: Not available.

### 2. Trends & Shifts In The Market

| Shift Category | Description of Change | The Window of Opportunity |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Unmanaged AI use at work | Employees adopt AI before the company sets rules. The site's own line: "Your team is already using AI." | A short, usable AI policy and rollout kit gets leaders from no rules to clear rules in one sitting. It is also a free entry point to paid work. |
| Client-data privacy in regulated work | Law, accounting and mortgage firms handle confidential data and cannot send it to public AI services. Open-weight models can now run inside a firm's own network. | Private AI for firms of about 3 to 25 people is a defined offer with a named buyer. Large providers rarely serve firms this small. |
| Build in-house over buy | Leaders are questioning the "build trap" and want to build AI capability themselves rather than hand it to vendors. | Advisory and workshops that teach leaders to build their own AI chief of staff fit this shift. They deliver capability the leader keeps. |
| Model churn and vendor lock-in | Models change fast, and most chat tools forget the business after each session. | An owned, model-agnostic "company brain" in plain files keeps the knowledge and lets the client switch models without loss. |

*Gap: no regulatory or dated external sources were provided. Confirm each shift with buyer conversations before it goes on the website.*

### 3. Landscape Map & Differentiation

**Category context:** Acme Advisory sits in AI consulting and advisory, next to AI governance. It also sells small software-style tools and workshops. The site claims no single category, so the market cannot place it yet. Brand awareness is low and unmeasured. Most competitors use generic "AI strategy and transformation" language, which leaves room for a sharper, narrower claim.

| Alternate Solution | Status Quo Limitation | Core Limitation / Why We Win |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Strategy houses | Board-level brand and scale. Slow, costly and built for large enterprises. | Acme Advisory offers senior attention, faster starts and prices a small company can afford. Pricing is unpublished, so confirm this edge. |
| Large consultancies and integrators | Strong on governance, controls and delivery scale. Heavy engagements and rotating teams. | Smaller, hands-on work led by one operator who has run the function. |
| AI boutiques and fractional teams | Deep engineering and build skill. Often light on product, positioning and adoption. | Acme Advisory leads with product judgment and team adoption, not only build. |
| Solo fractional AI executives | Named senior operators with published fees. One example starts at USD 80,000 for consulting and USD 30,000 a month for a fractional seat, with a six-month minimum. Capped client counts. | Buyers below that price floor, or those wanting bounded, independent work, are underserved. |
| AI governance software | Cheap and quick for policy and compliance. Does not build capability or change how people work. | Policy plus rollout and hands-on training, with a free generator as the entry point. |
| Internal teams | Close to the business. Short on time and AI experience, and slow to start. | An experienced outside operator speeds up the first 90 days. Needs proof. |
| Public chatbots, unmanaged | Free and instant. They forget the business, expose client data and lock the company into one vendor. | Owned memory in plain files, model choice, and models that run inside the office. |

**Weak spot:** Acme Advisory has no case studies, customer logos or measured outcomes. Every "why we win" claim above is a position, not yet a proven fact. The founder's track record is the only hard-to-copy asset, and it does not scale past one person.

### Positioning Summary: The Sweet Spot

**Sweet spot (draft, founder to confirm):** Owner-led firms of about 3 to 25 people, especially regulated professional practices, that want to use AI without exposing client data and cannot afford enterprise consulting or a full-time AI executive. Acme Advisory helps them adopt AI safely in weeks. A former product executive does the work hands-on, and the client keeps the data, the files and the choice of model.

**Core edge against incumbents:**
- **Operator credibility:** the advice comes from someone who has run the function.
- **Ownership:** plain files, swappable models and private deployment, so there is no lock-in.
- **Right-sized and bounded:** clear scope and a clear buyer, priced for firms the large providers skip.

**Decision needed from the founder:** Private AI is the most defined offer, but the homepage speaks to product and revenue leaders. Pick one lead offer and one primary buyer before the website and messaging are rewritten.

### Buying Triggers
All triggers are hypotheses inferred from the site's messaging. *Validate* each with the founder's real deals.

- **Trigger 1:** The owner discovers staff are pasting client material into public AI tools, or a client asks how the firm handles data and AI.
- **Trigger 2:** A hiring push. The site speaks to "any company that hires faster than it can explain itself."
- **Trigger 3:** Annual planning, when leadership has to commit to an AI roadmap. The site's offsite is framed around a 2027 AI roadmap.
- **Trigger 4:** A professional body, insurer or client questionnaire asks for a written AI policy.
- **Trigger 5:** A disappointing AI trial. The team used a chatbot, got little value and now wants a structured approach.

#### Value Driver: Use AI on Client Work Without Client Data Leaving the Office

1. **Customer Challenge:** The owner of a small regulated firm knows AI saves time. Staff already use public AI tools to get work done. The owner cannot see what client information goes into them. If a client asks where their data goes, the owner has no clean answer. Professional duty and liability sit with the owner personally.

2. **Status Quo:**
   - Staff use public chatbots on their own, with no approval.
   - There is either no written AI rule, or a rule nobody reads.
   - The owner's choices today are to ban AI and lose the gains, or to look away and carry the risk.
   - Some firms try a tool, get little value, and stall.

3. **Cost of Inaction:**
   - Client information keeps flowing into tools the firm does not control, and the exposure grows with every new use.
   - The firm cannot answer a client, insurer or professional body that asks about AI and data.
   - A ban pushes use underground. A free-for-all keeps the risk. Either way, competitors who solve this first gain the productivity.
   - Dollar or hour figures: **Not available.** No customer data exists. A rep should ask the buyer to size it (see Discovery Prompts). Do not publish a number until a real client supplies one.

4. **Our Distinct Advantage:**
   - The Private AI offer runs AI models **inside the client's own office**, so client information is not sent to outside services.
   - It is built for one buyer: firms of about 3 to 25 people. It is not a scaled-down enterprise product.
   - It pairs the setup with a written policy and a rollout, so the team changes how it works. The software alone does not do that.
   - The founder is an operator who says he has run the product function and still builds AI agents.
   - *Validate:* the site frames this as a unique fit for small regulated firms. Do not claim "only" in public copy until compared against real alternatives in deals.

5. **Future State:**
   - The team uses AI openly, on real client work, inside approved boundaries.
   - Client data stays in the firm's own walls.
   - The owner can tell a client exactly where their information goes.
   - A one-page policy is in place, and the team follows it because the approved option is easier than the public one.

6. **Proof Points:**
   - **Logical:** if models run inside the office, client information has no outside path to leave through. This is the core reason to believe.
   - **Site claim:** a stated size band (3 to 25 people), a defined timeline and stated disqualifiers on the Private AI page. The disqualifiers were not captured in the crawl. *Validate and add.*
   - **Low-risk entry:** the free AI Use Policy Generator lets a buyer start with no spend and see how the firm thinks.
   - **Operator credibility:** about 25 years in business software, including a senior product role at a company with a self-reported $1B exit. Tenure is stated inconsistently across the site (20 vs 25 years). Fix before using.
   - **Customer proof:** Not available. No case studies, logos or measured outcomes exist. This is the biggest gap for this driver. Even one anonymized firm story would help.

7. **Discovery Prompts:**
   - "If a client asked you tomorrow exactly where their information goes when your team uses AI, what would you tell them?"
   - "How do you know which AI tools your team used on client files last month?"
   - "When someone on your team finds an AI shortcut that saves two hours, what happens to it today? Does it get approved, hidden or banned?"

#### Value Driver: Company Knowledge That New Hires and AI Assistants Can Use From Day One

1. **Customer Challenge:** In a small firm, how the business really works lives in a few people's heads. Every new hire takes months to absorb it. AI tools make this worse. They forget the business every session, so each chat starts from zero.

2. **Status Quo:**
   - Senior people answer the same questions again and again.
   - Documents are scattered across inboxes, shared drives and personal notes.
   - AI use is ad hoc. Each person writes their own prompts and re-explains the firm every time.
   - Any knowledge put into a vendor's tool stays there, so switching later means starting over.

3. **Cost of Inaction:**
   - Each hire stays slow to produce while senior staff lose time coaching.
   - When a key person leaves, their knowledge leaves with them.
   - AI stays shallow because it never learns the business, so the gains stay small.
   - Locking knowledge inside one vendor makes the firm dependent on that vendor's pricing and choices.
   - Dollar or hour figures: **Not available.** The buyer can size this with their own ramp-up time and senior hours (see Discovery Prompts).

4. **Our Distinct Advantage:**
   - The 10x Employee approach builds an AI operating system on **plain files the client owns**.
   - An assistant that remembers the business and improves with use, instead of starting from zero.
   - It is model-agnostic. The firm can swap AI models later and lose nothing, because the knowledge is in the firm's files, not the vendor's system.
   - It is set up by someone who has run the function, not a tool vendor selling a license.
   - *Validate:* confirm in a real engagement that the plain-file design works as described.

5. **Future State:**
   - New hires get answers on day one from a system that knows how the firm works.
   - Senior staff stop answering the same questions.
   - The firm's knowledge sits in files it owns and can move at any time.
   - AI gets more useful each month, and a model change is a swap, not a rebuild.

6. **Proof Points:**
   - **Logical:** knowledge in files the client owns cannot be held hostage by a vendor, and any model can read it.
   - **Site claim:** the offer is built around ownership and model freedom. The site speaks to any company that "hires faster than it can explain itself."
   - **Operator credibility:** the founder's product leadership background and his claim that he still builds AI agents. This is self-reported.
   - **Customer proof, ramp-up time saved, hours returned to senior staff:** Not available. No measured outcomes exist in the documents.

7. **Discovery Prompts:**
   - "Think of your last hire. What did they still not know after 90 days, and who ended up teaching them?"
   - "If your two most experienced people were out for a month, what would the firm struggle to answer?"
   - "When you switch AI tools, what do you lose? What would you have to rebuild?"

---

A full-time AI lead is out of reach. The owner has no time to research models, so the choice is to guess, delegate to a tech-savvy employee, or wait.

This comes from third-party research in the market overview. *Validate against current prices before using publicly.*
   - **Low-risk entry:** free tools (AI Chief of Staff, AI Use Policy Generator, PositioningHQ) let a buyer test the thinking at no cost.

### Moat 1: Private AI Scoped for a Small Regulated Firm

#### 1. Description of the Advantage
- **What it is:** AI models run inside the client's own office, so client information is not sent to outside services. The offer is paired with a written policy and a team rollout. It is built for one buyer: owners and managing partners of regulated firms of about 3 to 25 people.
- **The "Unfair" Element:**
  - **Economics:** Large consultancies and enterprise providers are priced and scoped for big budgets. A firm of 10 people is not worth their sales cost, so they tend to ignore it.
  - **Incentives:** Public AI tool vendors profit when data flows through their systems. A "keep it in the office" design cuts against their model.
  - **Adoption:** Governance software gives a policy template. It does not change how staff work. The combined setup, policy and rollout is a service, not a license.
  - **Honest limit:** A larger rival could copy the architecture. The defense is a narrow focus, a small-firm price point and fast delivery, which only works if those are proven. *Validate:* do not claim "only" in public copy until compared with real alternatives in deals.

#### 2. Why Customers Care (The "So What?")
- **Value Translation:**
  - The owner can say yes to AI on client work without carrying unseen risk personally.
  - The owner has a clear answer when a client, insurer or professional body asks where client data goes.
  - Staff stop using public tools in secret, because the approved option is easier.
  - Dollar and hour figures: **Not available.** Ask the buyer to size them in discovery.
- **The Strategic Shift:**
  - **Lagging:** The owner finds out about AI use after the fact, by accident or after a client complaint. The only options are a ban or looking away.
  - **Leading:** The owner sets the boundaries first. AI is used openly, and data flow is known and explainable before anyone asks.

#### 3. Proof Points (Evidence)
- **Architecture argument (logical):** If models run inside the office, client information has no outside path to leave through. Build a one-page data-flow diagram to show this. *To build.*
- **Scope proof (site claim):** The Private AI page states a size band, a defined timeline and disqualifiers. The disqualifiers were not captured in the crawl. *Validate and add. Confirm the timeline before publishing.*
- **Low-risk entry:** The free AI Use Policy Generator lets a buyer test the thinking with no spend.
- **Customer proof:** Not available. One anonymized firm story with a before-and-after on data handling would be the strongest asset for this moat.

#### 4. Discovery Prompts (The "Trap" Questions)
- "If a client's lawyer or insurer asked for a written record of which AI tools touched their file last quarter, what could you hand over?"
- "When your team finds an AI shortcut that works, what is the route for getting it approved, and how long does that take?"
- "Which providers have you talked to about AI, and what did they say about a firm your size?" *(Listen for being ignored, being pitched enterprise scope, or being handed a template.)*

### Moat 2: Company Knowledge in Plain Files the Client Owns

#### 1. Description of the Advantage
- **What it is:** The 10x Employee approach builds an AI operating system on plain files the client owns. The assistant remembers how the business works and improves with use. It is model-agnostic: the firm can swap AI models and keep everything.
- **The "Unfair" Element:**
  - **Business-model conflict:** Vendors who sell an AI tool earn more when the firm's knowledge sits inside their system. Offering true portability weakens their own lock-in, so they are unlikely to copy it.
  - **Design choice, not a feature:** Ownership and portability are built into the structure from day one. A vendor cannot easily add this later to a product built around its own storage.
  - **Honest limit:** Plain files are not secret technology. A consultancy could copy the approach. The edge holds only if it is paired with strong setup and adoption work. *Validate:* confirm in a real engagement that the design works as described.

#### 2. Why Customers Care (The "So What?")
- **Value Translation:**
  - New hires get answers from day one instead of spending months absorbing how the firm works.
  - Senior people stop answering the same questions.
  - A key person leaving no longer takes the firm's knowledge with them.
  - A change of AI model, or a change in a vendor's pricing, is a swap and not a rebuild.
  - Dollar and hour figures: **Not available.** The buyer can size them from ramp-up time and senior hours.
- **The Strategic Shift:**
  - **Lagging:** Knowledge sits in heads and scattered inboxes. Each AI chat starts from zero. Each vendor choice is a one-way door.
  - **Leading:** The firm's knowledge is a growing asset it owns. AI gets more useful each month, and the firm picks the best model at any time.

#### 3. Proof Points (Evidence)
- **Portability test (to build):** Run a live demo where the same set of client-owned files is read by two different AI models with no rework. This shows the claim instead of stating it.
- **Ownership by design (logical):** Plain files the client holds cannot be held hostage by a vendor, and any model can read them.
- **Site claim:** The offer is built around ownership and model freedom, and speaks to any company that "hires faster than it can explain itself."
- **Customer proof, ramp-up time saved, senior hours returned:** Not available. Capture one baseline, such as days to first useful work from a new hire, before and after any real engagement.

#### 4. Discovery Prompts (The "Trap" Questions)
- "If you decided next year to change AI tools, what would you have to rebuild, and who would do it?"
- "Where does the knowledge your assistant has built up about your business actually live, and who owns it?"
- "Think of your last hire. What did they still not know after 90 days, and who taught them?"

---

### Moat 3: Operator-Led Delivery by Someone Who Has Run the Function

#### 1. Description of the Advantage
- **What it is:** Advice and setup delivered directly by a founder who says he has run a product function and still builds AI agents. Engagements are bounded and independent, with no tie to a software vendor. The aim is a working setup the firm owns, not a deck.
- **The "Unfair" Element:**
  - **Earned, not bought:** Roughly 25 years in business software, including senior product and technology roles, cannot be copied by a competitor in a hiring cycle. All of it is self-reported.
  - **Independence:** Providers tied to software they implement have a reason to recommend it. A bounded, independent engagement has no such conflict.
  - **Honest limit:** This is the weakest moat structurally. It rests on one person and does not scale. It is a good reason to buy, not a defense once a larger firm decides to target small buyers. Fix the tenure inconsistency (20 vs 25 years) before using it publicly.

#### 2. Why Customers Care (The "So What?")
- **Value Translation:**
  - The owner gets senior judgment without hiring a full-time AI lead.
  - The firm's best people go back to client work instead of researching models.
  - Advice is scoped to a small team, so the budget goes to something running, not to overhead.
  - Dollar and hour figures: **Not available.**
- **The Strategic Shift:**
  - **Lagging:** AI is a side project for a tech-savvy employee. Trials stall and the plan is put off a year.
  - **Leading:** Leadership holds a clear annual AI plan sized to the firm, and the team follows it.

#### 3. Proof Points (Evidence)
- **Founder track record (self-reported):** Product leadership roles, including one at a company with a self-reported $1B exit. Verify and cite exactly.
- **Free tools as a work sample:** AI Chief of Staff, AI Use Policy Generator and PositioningHQ let a buyer judge the thinking before paying.
- **Price-floor gap (third-party research):** The closest solo rival publishes fees of USD 80,000 and up for consulting, with a six-month minimum on a monthly seat. This suggests an opening for bounded work below that floor. *Validate against current prices before using publicly. Acme Advisory pricing is not published.*
- **Customer proof:** Not available.

#### 4. Discovery Prompts (The "Trap" Questions)
- "Who at your firm owns the AI question today, and what are they not doing because of it?"
- "Of the advisors you have spoken to, who would be the one actually doing the work, and what else do they sell you?"
- "What did your last AI trial produce, and why did it stop?"

### 1. Internal Positioning Statement

| Field | Positioning Component |
| :--- | :--- |
| **For** | Owners and managing partners of regulated professional firms of about 3 to 25 people (law, accounting, mortgage brokerage and similar) who want their team to use AI on client work without client information leaving the office. |
| **Who are currently dissatisfied with** | Staff using public AI chatbots with no approved alternative and no rules anyone follows. The only options they see are to ban AI and lose the gains, or look away and carry the risk. Large consultancies are scoped and priced for enterprises and tend to ignore firms this size. |
| **Our Product is a** | Private AI setup for small regulated firms. AI models run inside the firm's own office, with a written policy and a team rollout included. |
| **That provides** | The productivity gains of AI with client data staying inside the firm. The owner can tell any client, insurer or professional body exactly where information goes. |
| **Unlike** | Enterprise-scoped consultancies that deliver slide decks, and policy-only governance software that hands over a template and changes no habits. |
| **We** | Put AI inside your office and make sure your team uses it. Company knowledge sits in plain files you own, so you can switch AI models without losing anything. A former product executive does the work hands-on. |

**Reasons to believe (use only what is true today)**
- **Logical:** if models run inside the office, client information has no outside path to leave through.
- **Logical:** knowledge in plain files the client holds cannot be held hostage by a vendor, and any model can read it.
- **Site claim, self-reported:** the founder has run a product function and still builds AI agents. Fix the tenure inconsistency (20 vs 25 years) before using it.
- **Low-risk entry:** free tools, including the AI Use Policy Generator, let a buyer test the thinking before paying.
- **Customer proof:** Not available. This is the biggest gap in the statement.

**Why this statement and not another**
- It is the only offer in the documents with a named buyer, a size band and a concrete pain.
- Governance is now crowded (Section 6). Private deployment plus adoption for firms this small is a narrower claim and easier to defend.
- The solo advisor model is not unique. Another solo operator sells it too. So the statement leads with the fit and the setup, not with "one senior advisor."

> **Why now:** Employees adopt AI before companies set rules. Open-weight models can now run inside a firm's own network. Clients, insurers and professional bodies are starting to ask about AI and data. Models change fast, so owned and portable company knowledge matters more every quarter.

Vendors who sell AI tools lose their lock-in if they copy the portability. Large providers cannot serve this size profitably. There are no case studies or measured outcomes yet, so the first priority is proof: one anonymized firm story, a data-flow diagram and a live portability demo.

### 1. Market & Analyst Sentiment Summary

Public proof for Acme Advisory is very thin. There are no third-party reviews, no analyst coverage and no press articles. Most public material is about Sam Rivera, not the company. His site cites 25 years building business software companies and helping scale a past employer to a $1B exit as VP of Product. A conference attendee posted that he spoke at ProductCamp Vancouver 2026 and walked the audience through how technology has evolved since the start of the internet. Today, buyers have credentials and one testimonial to go on. They have no body of reviews.

Search risk: "Parallel" is a common name. Reviews for an unrelated document-onboarding tool, and pages about other companies with the same name, show up in search. None of it is about Acme Advisory. Do not cite it. Always write "Acme Advisory" in full when asking for reviews.

- No analyst category for this kind of offer was found in the documents. I will not invent one.
- Directory-style lists of Vancouver AI strategy firms exist. I could not confirm Acme Advisory is on any of them.
- One directory entry (Crunchbase) describes Sam's roles. It is not coverage and may be out of date.

**What this means:** Your positioning cannot lean on third-party validation yet. Lean on founder experience, a specific method and a fast path to first results. Close the proof gap before you scale messaging.

### 3. Notable Verified Quotes

Only one verified quote exists.

> "an effective way to get your sales & marketing teams using AI properly from day one."
> Reza Varzidehkar, Founder, OVOU. Source: product.example, undated. About the PositioningHQ workshop only.

- **The "Aha!" in it:** AI use is right from day one, not after months of trial and error. Use this as a theme in messaging, tied to the workshop.
- **Not usable as quotes:** The ProductCamp attendee's post is a paraphrase, not a quote about outcomes. Review sites, Reddit and analyst sources returned nothing for Acme Advisory.

### Priority Fixes

| Gap | Action | Why it matters |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| No reviews anywhere | Collect 3 to 5 written reviews from past clients. Ask for a G2 or Clutch listing under "Acme Advisory". | Fastest fix for a buyer who searches before they call. |
| One undated testimonial, no figures | Go back to the OVOU founder. Ask for a date and one number, such as hours saved or time to rollout. | Turns a nice quote into a verifiable outcome. |
| No before and after data | After each engagement, record 2 to 3 metrics: win rate, sales cycle, hours saved. | The evidence table needs numbers to work. |
| No proof for AI strategy, governance or ISO 42001 offers | Ask one client per offer for a short quote. | The current quote covers only the workshop. |
| LinkedIn recommendations unchecked | Review them by hand and ask permission to reuse. | They may already hold usable praise. |
